templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Dash pair around a supplementary element
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation between subject and verb
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a participial opener
items.passage: Built in 1495 for Askia Mohammad I, ruler of the Songhai Empire, the Tomb of Askia in Gao, Mali, is a pyramidal structure constructed almost entirely of ______ the wooden beams that protrude from its sides as permanent scaffolding, local masons periodically replaster the monument’s exterior to protect it from erosion.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “constructed almost entirely of mud.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Using the wooden beams that protrude from its sides as permanent scaffolding,” which describes its subject, “local masons,” and then gives the main verb, “replaster.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma attaches “using the wooden beams that protrude from its sides as permanent scaffolding” to the first clause, so the main clause “local masons periodically replaster the monument’s exterior” follows it with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “mud using the wooden beams ...” runs the participial phrase into the first clause, and the main clause “local masons periodically replaster the monument’s exterior” is then joined to it with only a comma.

D.why_wrong: “And” cannot join the noun “mud” to a participial phrase, and the main clause “local masons periodically replaster the monument’s exterior” is still attached to the first main clause with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: history and architecture (Tomb of Askia, Gao). Band 6 (models 1b97cce9 tombs. Built, 73a6603c temperature. Adding): 12-word participial opener before clause 2's subject; the comma version reads as a modifier of the first clause until “local masons periodically replaster.” No semicolon option (it would be a twin of the period).

band7.why: 12-word participial opener that also reads as a modifier of “constructed” (1b97cce9 shape); a band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long past-participle opener
items.passage: In the early twentieth century, Zulu migrant workers in South Africa’s cities and mining centers developed a style of unaccompanied choral singing called ______ from a Zulu verb meaning “to walk softly” or “to tread carefully,” the style’s name evokes the light, controlled dance steps that accompany the singing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “a style of unaccompanied choral singing called isicathamiya.” The second sentence opens with a past-participial phrase (“Derived from a Zulu verb ...”) that describes its subject, “the style’s name,” and then gives the main verb, “evokes.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “derived from a Zulu verb ...” look like a description of “isicathamiya,” but then the main clause “the style’s name evokes the light, controlled dance steps” is joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “isicathamiya derived from a Zulu verb ...” attaches the phrase to the first clause, and the main clause “the style’s name evokes ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “Which was derived” turns the phrase into a relative clause describing “isicathamiya,” so the main clause “the style’s name evokes ...” is still joined to the first main clause with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: arts (isicathamiya, South African choral singing). Band-7 checks (band7/boundaries.md section 6): 13-word past-participle opener that reads naturally on clause 1's last noun (“isicathamiya, derived from ...”); the comma, glued and which-was options hold until “the style’s name evokes,” 12 words after the blank; cue outside a 6-word window; one-sentence run of 49 words; reasoning steps 3. Option menu of 4b424102 (comma, period, glued, added relative).
band7_moves: 13-word past-participle opener that could describe clause 1's last noun
comma, glued and which-was options read as descriptions of isicathamiya until the splice 12 words later

band7.why: 13-word past-participle opener that hangs naturally on “isicathamiya” until “the style’s name evokes” (a872c60a, ba8ebf49 shape); comma, glued and which-was options all fail far from the blank.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, contrast with the previous sentence
items.passage: In most armadillos, the bony carapace is connected to the body along the entire length of the animal’s back. The pink fairy armadillo, a diminutive burrowing species endemic to central Argentina, is a striking ______ its carapace is attached to the body solely by a thin membrane running along the animal’s spine.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence says that in most armadillos “the bony carapace is connected to the body along the entire length of the animal’s back.” The second sentence sets the pink fairy armadillo against this, so “however” belongs with the first main clause, “The pink fairy armadillo ... is a striking exception,” and is set off with a comma. A semicolon then joins that clause to the second main clause, “its carapace is attached to the body solely by a thin membrane running along the animal’s spine,” which explains the exception.

B.why_wrong: Placing “however” at the start of the second clause would contrast “its carapace is attached ... solely by a thin membrane” with the claim that the armadillo is an exception, but that detail is what makes it an exception, not a contrast to it. The contrast is with the previous sentence.

C.why_wrong: With commas on both sides of “however,” the main clauses “The pink fairy armadillo ... is a striking exception” and “its carapace is attached ...” are joined with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the main clauses “The pink fairy armadillo ... is a striking exception however” and “its carapace is attached ...” are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (pink fairy armadillo, shell attached by a thin membrane along the spine; Wikipedia states the membrane detail). Band-7 checks: clause 1 qualifies the previous sentence (an exception to the rule it states); clause 2 elaborates clause 1 and carries no contrast of its own, so the textbook “; however,” placement fails only on meaning against the previous sentence (be37d4ae, c06af4d8 menu). Logic-wrong distractor present; cue (the previous sentence) outside the 6-word window.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence
logic-wrong “; however,” option (the pattern students are taught)
clause 2 elaborates clause 1, so only the previous sentence decides the side

band7.why: Adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence; the textbook “; however,” fails only on meaning (c06af4d8, be37d4ae). Caveat: clause 1 uses the noun “exception” rather than CB's negation (“not the first”, “doesn’t ... single-handedly”), so the adverb's home is a little more visible than in the models.

items.subtype: Transitional adverb opening clause 2 after a negative clause (not X; rather, Y), with an opener before clause 2’s subject
items.passage: Classical Somali poetry, long used to settle disputes and comment on political affairs, follows strict rules of sound. A poet may not switch to a different alliterating sound partway through a ______ after selecting one sound at the beginning, the poet must start at least one word in every line of the composition with that sound.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first main clause says what a poet may not do (“A poet may not switch to a different alliterating sound partway through a poem”), and the second says what the poet must do instead (“the poet must start at least one word in every line of the composition with that sound”). “Rather” introduces that alternative, so it belongs at the start of the second main clause, followed by a comma, and a semicolon joins the two main clauses.

A.recipe: misplaced boundary (adverb on the wrong side)
A.why_wrong: This places “rather” at the end of the first clause, but “rather” introduces what the poet must do instead, “the poet must start at least one word in every line of the composition with that sound,” so it must open the second clause, after the semicolon.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the main clauses “A poet may not switch to a different alliterating sound partway through a poem” and “the poet must start at least one word in every line of the composition with that sound” are fused into a run-on sentence.

D.why_wrong: With commas on both sides of “rather,” the main clauses “A poet may not switch to a different alliterating sound partway through a poem” and “the poet must start at least one word in every line of the composition with that sound” are joined with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: literature and language (classical Somali poetry, one alliterating sound held through the poem). Replaced in review: the Manyōshū draft duplicated live w4b3_04. Band 6 (a9e5b788 shape: “; rather,” after a negative clause, then a 7-word opener, “after selecting one sound at the beginning,” before clause 2’s subject “the poet”). Band 7 never uses rather (band7/boundaries.md 5).

band7.why: “; rather,” after a negative clause with an opener before clause 2’s subject (a9e5b788, band 6); band 7 never uses rather, so a band-6 target, met.

fixes: replaced the Manyōshū subject (duplicate of live boundaries.S1_adverb.hard.w4b3_04) with classical Somali alliterative poetry on the same template, tier and band_target; new passage, options, explanation, distractors and notes; claim appended to claims.txt and the old claim withdrawn
review.note: blind answer and agreement refer to the original Manyōshū draft (C, agreed); replacement written by the reviewer, key C

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase with a relative clause
items.passage: Caño Cristales, a river in central Colombia, is sometimes called the River of Five Colors. Its most spectacular hue, the vivid red that streaks the riverbed between roughly July and November, originates from an unexpected ______ aquatic plant, Macarenia clavigera, whose leaves, when exposed to intense sunlight in shallow water, turn a brilliant crimson.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “Its most spectacular hue ... originates from an unexpected source” is complete and announces something that the rest of the sentence names: “an aquatic plant, Macarenia clavigera, whose leaves ... turn a brilliant crimson.” A colon is used to introduce such an explanation, and it correctly joins a main clause to a phrase that is not a main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “an aquatic plant, Macarenia clavigera, whose leaves ... turn a brilliant crimson” has no main verb of its own (“turn” belongs to the relative clause), so it can’t stand after a semicolon.

C.why_wrong: “It is an aquatic plant ...” is a main clause, so joining it to the main clause “Its most spectacular hue ... originates from an unexpected source” with only a comma creates a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: The period makes “An aquatic plant, Macarenia clavigera, whose leaves ... turn a brilliant crimson” a separate sentence, but it is a fragment: its only verb, “turn,” is inside a relative clause.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Caño Cristales, Macarenia clavigera). Band-7 checks (e9aee0d8, f30a478e shape): clause 1 ends on an announcing phrase (“originates from an unexpected source”); the noun phrase after the blank carries a relative clause whose finite verb (“turn”) sits 14 words after the blank, behind an interrupter, so the period and semicolon versions read like sentences; added-word splice decoy (“it is”). No lone dash offered.
band7_moves: noun phrase after the colon carries a relative clause with a finite verb 14 words on
clause 1 ends on an announcing phrase

band7.why: Announcing clause 1 plus a noun phrase whose only finite verb sits inside a relative clause 14 words on (e9aee0d8, f30a478e); semicolon and period read like sentence joins until then.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a list
items.passage: The original handwritten Constitution of India, adopted in 1949, was decorated by painter Nandalal Bose and his students. Their illustrations draw on thousands of years of the subcontinent’s ______ a seal from the ancient city of Mohenjo-daro, a scene from the epic Ramayana, and Mahatma Gandhi’s 1930 Salt March.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “Their illustrations draw on thousands of years of the subcontinent’s history” is complete, and what follows is a list that specifies that history: “a seal from the ancient city of Mohenjo-daro, a scene from the epic Ramayana, and Mahatma Gandhi’s 1930 Salt March.” A colon is used to introduce such a list.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but the list “a seal from the ancient city of Mohenjo-daro, a scene ..., and Mahatma Gandhi’s 1930 Salt March” has no verb, so it can’t stand after a semicolon.

B.why_wrong: The period makes the list “A seal from the ancient city of Mohenjo-daro, a scene ..., and Mahatma Gandhi’s 1930 Salt March” a separate sentence, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the list runs straight on from “history,” as if “the subcontinent’s history a seal from ...” were one noun phrase; a colon is needed to introduce the list.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Nandalal Bose's illustrations for the Constitution of India, 1950). Band 6 (c468db1c menu: period, semicolon, no mark, colon before a list of specified items). No lone dash offered.

band7.why: Colon before a list of specified items on c468db1c's menu (period, semicolon, no mark); plain band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: No punctuation with a restrictive appositive (not a person), with a second slot before the verb
items.passage: Sea angels, small swimming snails that lose their shells soon after hatching, include dozens of species distributed throughout the world’s oceans. Research has shown that the sea ______ almost exclusively on a single shelled relative, the sea butterfly Limacina helicina, which it captures with tentacles that extend from its mouth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Because there are “dozens of species” of sea angels, the name “Clione limacina” is essential: it tells which sea angel the research is about. An essential (restrictive) appositive is not set off with commas, and no comma separates the subject “the sea angel Clione limacina” from its verb, “preys.”

B.why_wrong: The commas treat “Clione limacina” as extra information, but the passage says sea angels include dozens of species, so the name is needed to identify which one preys on Limacina helicina.

C.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject “the sea angel Clione limacina” from its verb, “preys.”

D.why_wrong: The comma separates “the sea angel” from the name that identifies it, and the name is essential, so no punctuation belongs there.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (sea angel Clione limacina feeding on Limacina helicina). Band-7 checks: non-person restrictive appositive (“the sea angel Clione limacina,” the 59a246dc setting) whose essentialness rests on the previous sentence (“dozens of species”), plus a second slot before the verb (0a114526). S4_restrictive is exempt from the local-window check.
band7_moves: non-person restrictive appositive with an article (the sea angel Clione limacina)
the reason the name is essential sits in the previous sentence
second slot between the name and the verb

band7.why: Non-person restrictive appositive whose essentialness rests on the previous sentence (“dozens of species”), plus a second slot before the verb (59a246dc, 0a114526).

items.subtype: No punctuation with a restrictive appositive (descriptor + name)
items.passage: Carved into a horseshoe-shaped cliff in western India, the Ajanta Caves contain some of the finest surviving examples of ancient Indian painting. In 1819, while hunting a tiger in the surrounding hills, British cavalry ______ noticed the overgrown entrance to one of the caves, which had been abandoned for more than a millennium.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “British cavalry officer John Smith” is the subject of the sentence. The name “John Smith” is essential: it identifies which British cavalry officer is meant, so it is not set off with commas. No punctuation should separate the subject from its verb, “noticed.”

A.why_wrong: The commas treat “John Smith” as extra information, but the name is needed to identify which officer noticed the cave, so it should not be set off from “British cavalry officer.”

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject “British cavalry officer John Smith” from its verb, “noticed.”

D.why_wrong: The comma separates the title “British cavalry officer” from the name that identifies the officer; the two form one unit and take no punctuation.

items.notes: Subject: history and art (Ajanta Caves, John Smith of the Madras cavalry, April 1819). Band 6 (4dcedc31, 594b4a94): article-less descriptor + name as subject, introductory participial phrase before it so a comma feels natural.

band7.why: Article-less descriptor + name as subject after an introductory phrase (4dcedc31, 594b4a94); band-6 target, met.

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair around an element that contains parentheses
items.passage: In 1636, Emperor Fasilides established the town of Gondar as the capital of Ethiopia. Over the following century, the fortified royal compound he founded there—known today as Fasil Ghebbi (“Fasil’s compound” in ______ expanded to include castles, churches, a library, and a banquet hall commissioned by his successors.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The supplementary element “known today as Fasil Ghebbi (“Fasil’s compound” in Amharic)” is set off from the rest of the sentence by a dash that opens it after “there.” The parenthetical gloss inside that element must be closed first, with “)”, and then the element itself must be closed with a second dash so that the subject, “the fortified royal compound he founded there,” connects to its verb, “expanded.”

A.why_wrong: The element was opened with a dash after “there,” so it must be closed with a dash, not a comma.

B.why_wrong: The parenthetical “(“Fasil’s compound” in Amharic)” sits inside the dash element, so the parenthesis must be closed before the dash; placing the dash first leaves the two marks crossed.

C.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the element that opened with a dash after “there” is never closed, so “expanded” is cut off from its subject, “the fortified royal compound.”

items.notes: Subject: history and architecture (Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar). Band-7 checks (83898524 nesting): a parenthetical gloss sits inside the dash element, so the option must close both levels in the right order; the opening dash is 8 words before the blank (7 to 10 is the band-7 range); the verb that the element interrupts comes after the blank; run of 34 words. Every option differs only in the order and type of marks.
band7_moves: second nesting level (parentheses) inside the dash element
partner dash 8 words before the blank
options mix the two levels (comma, crossed marks, missing dash)

band7.why: Two nesting levels (parenthetical inside a dash element); the opening dash is 8 words back, outside the local window (83898524 menu).

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas, plus a comma before an appositive inside the option
items.passage: Huapango, a musical tradition from the Huasteca region of eastern Mexico, is customarily performed by a trio: a violin, which carries the melody and improvises ornamental flourishes between ______ a small five-string guitar that provides a steady rhythmic accompaniment; and a huapanguera, a larger eight-string guitar that supplies the bass line.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The colon introduces a list of the trio’s three instruments, and each item contains internal commas (“a violin, which carries the melody ...”), so the items are separated by semicolons, as the semicolon before “and a huapanguera” confirms. A semicolon therefore follows “verses.” Within the second item, a comma is needed after “a jarana huasteca” to set off the explanation that follows it, “a small five-string guitar that provides a steady rhythmic accompaniment.”

A.why_wrong: Because the items contain commas and the last item is introduced with a semicolon (“; and a huapanguera”), the boundary between the first and second items must also be a semicolon; a comma leaves it unclear where the violin’s item ends.

C.why_wrong: The semicolon is right, but without a comma after “a jarana huasteca,” the explanation “a small five-string guitar that provides a steady rhythmic accompaniment” runs into the instrument’s name.

D.why_wrong: The list has already been introduced by a colon after “trio,” so a second colon can’t separate its items, and a semicolon after “a jarana huasteca” wrongly cuts that instrument off from its explanation.

items.notes: Subject: arts (huapango / son huasteco trio: violin, jarana huasteca, huapanguera). Band-7 checks (9c3630b9, db24ecc9): three long items, blank at the end of item 1, the revealing semicolon (“; and a huapanguera”) 10 words after the blank; a second rule inside the option (comma before the appositive that explains “a jarana huasteca”). Cue outside the 6-word window; run of 51 words.
band7_moves: blank in item 1, revealing semicolon later in the sentence
second rule inside the option (comma before an appositive)
items are long noun phrases with relative clauses

band7.why: Semicolon series with the blank at the end of item 1, the revealing semicolon 10 words later, and a second rule (comma before an appositive) inside the option (9c3630b9, db24ecc9).

items.subtype: Comma pair around an interrupter after a conjunction in a compound predicate
items.passage: Leatherbacks, the largest living sea turtles, subsist almost entirely on jellyfish, gelatinous animals that are mostly water and provide little nutrition. To satisfy its considerable energy requirements, a leatherback must spend much of its time ______ can consume hundreds of kilograms of jellyfish.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: feeding and, in a single day,
feeding and in a single day,
feeding and, in a single day
items.explanation: The phrase “in a single day” interrupts the compound predicate “must spend much of its time feeding and ... can consume hundreds of kilograms of jellyfish.” Because it is supplementary, it must be set off by a pair of commas, one before it and one after it.

B.why_wrong: The comma after “day” closes the interrupter, but without a comma after “and” to open it, the phrase is not properly set off.

C.why_wrong: The comma after “and” opens the interrupter, but without a comma after “day” to close it, “in a single day” runs into “can consume.”

D.why_wrong: The interrupter is opened with a dash but closed with a comma; a supplementary element must be set off by two marks of the same kind.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (leatherback sea turtles, jellyfish diet). S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official items (band7/boundaries.md section 5), so this cell is written as a strong band 6 on fdb16e20's shape (interrupter after “and” in a compound predicate, all four options carry the same words). band_target set to 6.

band7.why: S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 on fdb16e20's shape.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: In 1875, Bass Reeves became one of the first Black deputy US marshals west of the Mississippi River, apprehending fugitives throughout an immense territory that is now part of Oklahoma. Reeves had never learned to ______ he compensated by having each arrest warrant read aloud to him and memorizing its contents.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence joins two main clauses, “Reeves had never learned to read” and “he compensated by having each arrest warrant read aloud to him and memorizing its contents.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and shows the contrast between them.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses “Reeves had never learned to read” and “he compensated by having each arrest warrant read aloud to him ...”; the result is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: When a coordinating conjunction joins two main clauses of this length, a comma is conventionally placed before it.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: history (Bass Reeves, deputy US marshal, Indian Territory). Medium: the second clause opens with a pronoun subject; menu of 2.2 (comma, conjunction without comma, no mark, comma + but).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses, second opening with a short prepositional phrase
items.passage: Starting in the fourth century BCE, Anuradhapura served for over a millennium as the capital of an ancient Sinhalese kingdom in Sri Lanka. The city’s rulers constructed enormous reservoirs to capture rainfall during the monsoon ______ the dry months, an elaborate network of canals distributed the stored water to outlying rice paddies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “to capture rainfall during the monsoon season.” The second sentence opens with the prepositional phrase “During the dry months,” followed by its subject, “an elaborate network of canals,” and its verb, “distributed.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma lets “during the dry months” attach to the first clause, but then the main clause “an elaborate network of canals distributed ...” follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “the monsoon season during the dry months” reads as one phrase, which makes no sense, and the main clause “an elaborate network of canals distributed ...” is joined to the first with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two main clauses of this length, a comma is conventionally placed before it; without one, the sentence is not punctuated correctly.

items.notes: Subject: history (Anuradhapura reservoirs and canals, Sri Lanka). Medium: 4-word opener (2.10 In 1420 CE, 2.27 Prior to ...); the glued option is also meaning-wrong (rain cannot be captured in the monsoon season during the dry months).

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: Fado, a genre of song that emerged in the working-class neighborhoods of Lisbon, Portugal, in the 1820s, is characterized by melancholy themes of longing and loss. In 2011, UNESCO added fado to its list of the world’s intangible cultural ______ it as a living tradition that still flourishes in Lisbon’s intimate clubs and restaurants.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “In 2011, UNESCO added fado to its list of the world’s intangible cultural heritage” is followed by a participial phrase, “recognizing it as a living tradition ...,” that describes what UNESCO did in adding fado. A comma correctly separates the main clause from this supplementary phrase.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “recognizing it as a living tradition ...” is a participial phrase with no subject or main verb.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Recognizing it as a living tradition ...” a separate sentence, but it has no subject or main verb, so it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: “And” would join the main clause to a participial phrase as if they were parallel; with no subject or main verb after “and,” the sentence doesn’t hold together.

items.notes: Subject: arts (fado, UNESCO list 2011). Medium: trailing -ing phrase (2.4, 2.26 shape) with an added-and decoy in place of the model's no-mark option.

items.subtype: Closing comma of a participial phrase set off between subject and verb
items.passage: Rakugo, a traditional form of comic storytelling, has been performed in Japan since the seventeenth century. A rakugo performer, kneeling on a cushion and using only a folding fan and a small cotton ______ portrays every character in a narrative, indicating a change of speaker with a subtle turn of the head.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “kneeling on a cushion and using only a folding fan and a small cotton towel” interrupts the subject, “A rakugo performer,” and its verb, “portrays.” It opens with a comma after “performer,” so it must be closed with a comma after “towel.”

A.why_wrong: Without a comma after “towel,” the phrase that opened with a comma after “performer” is never closed.

C.why_wrong: The phrase opened with a comma, so it must close with a comma, not a dash.

D.why_wrong: “And” would join “portrays every character” to the descriptive phrase as if it were another action of the kneeling performer, leaving the sentence’s subject, “A rakugo performer,” without a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: literature and performance (rakugo, Japanese comic storytelling). Medium: partner comma 14 words before the blank (2.1 shape).

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory adjective phrase
items.passage: Finland’s government has long provided expectant mothers with a cardboard box of infant clothing, bedding, and other essential supplies. Available to any mother who attends a prenatal clinic by the end of her fourth month of ______ the box itself can function as a newborn’s first bed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The introductory phrase “Available to any mother who attends a prenatal clinic by the end of her fourth month of pregnancy” describes the subject of the sentence, “the box itself.” A comma is needed to separate this introductory phrase from the main clause it modifies.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory phrase runs into the subject: “her fourth month of pregnancy the box itself ...”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “Available to any mother who attends a prenatal clinic by the end of her fourth month of pregnancy” is a phrase with no main verb (“attends” belongs to the relative clause).

D.why_wrong: “And” would join the introductory phrase to the main clause as if they were parallel, but the phrase is not a clause; it describes the box.

items.notes: Subject: social science and public policy (Finland's maternity package, the baby box). Medium: 16-word introductory adjective phrase that contains its own relative clause (“who attends”), so the semicolon version can look like a clause boundary (2.20 shape: an essential modifier inside the opener).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: Launched in Brazil in 2003, the Bolsa Família program was designed to combat poverty in two ways at once. The monthly payments that the program provided to low-income families on the condition that their children attend school and receive regular ______ helped relieve immediate hardship while encouraging investment in the next generation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the long noun phrase “The monthly payments that the program provided to low-income families on the condition that their children attend school and receive regular vaccinations,” and its verb is “helped.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject, “The monthly payments ... regular vaccinations,” from its verb, “helped.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but the words before it are only a subject, with no main verb, and the words after it have no subject.

C.why_wrong: A single dash here has no role; it separates the subject from its verb, “helped.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (Bolsa Família, Brazil, 2003). Medium: 22-word subject with a restrictive relative clause and a condition clause before the blank, so a comma feels natural (2.11 shape).

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas
items.passage: Laxdæla saga, an Icelandic family saga composed in the thirteenth century, chronicles the life of the strong-willed Guðrún Ósvífursdóttir through four marriages: to Thorvald, a wealthy landowner whom she soon ______ Thord, who perished at sea; Bolli, the foster brother of the man she genuinely loved; and Thorkel, an influential chieftain who also drowned.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The colon introduces a list of Guðrún’s four husbands, and each item contains a comma (“Thorvald, a wealthy landowner whom she soon divorced”), so the items are separated by semicolons, as the semicolons after “sea” and “loved” confirm. A semicolon therefore follows “divorced.”

B.why_wrong: Because the items in this list contain commas, a comma after “divorced” would make it unclear where one item ends and the next begins; the rest of the list uses semicolons.

C.why_wrong: The list is already introduced by a colon after “marriages,” and a colon can’t separate items within a list.

D.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “whom she soon divorced Thord” makes Thord the object of “divorced,” and the first two items run together.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Laxdæla saga, Guðrún Ósvífursdóttir). Medium: complex series, blank at the end of item 1, revealing semicolons later (2.16 shape). The no-mark option also misreads (“divorced Thord”), a fair medium trap.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Each year at the start of the rainy season, tens of millions of red crabs on Christmas Island migrate from the forest to the coastline to reproduce. Park rangers temporarily block traffic and direct the migrating animals through tunnels constructed ______ the island’s roads.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The preposition “under” and its object, “the island’s roads,” form one phrase that tells where the tunnels were constructed. No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, and it can’t separate the preposition “under” from its object, “the island’s roads.”

C.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate the preposition “under” from its object, “the island’s roads.”

D.why_wrong: A dash can’t separate the preposition “under” from its object, “the island’s roads.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Christmas Island red crab migration, traffic closures and crab underpasses). Easy: local preposition-object boundary; four different marks.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Japanese artist Shiko Munakata won the top international prize for printmaking at the 1956 Venice Biennale. Because he was extremely nearsighted, Munakata carved his large woodblocks with his face just inches ______ the wood’s surface.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The preposition “from” and its object, “the wood’s surface,” form one phrase that tells how close Munakata’s face was to the wood. No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A dash can’t separate the preposition “from” from its object, “the wood’s surface.”

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, and it can’t separate the preposition “from” from its object.

D.why_wrong: A comma can’t separate the preposition “from” from its object, “the wood’s surface.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (Shiko Munakata, woodblock printmaker, 1956 Venice Biennale print prize). Easy: local preposition-object boundary (1.5, 1.22 menu).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Białowieża Forest, which straddles the border between Poland and Belarus, supports one of Europe’s largest populations of European bison. The animals had disappeared from the forest by the early ______ bison raised in captivity were reintroduced there in the 1950s.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence joins two main clauses, “The animals had disappeared from the forest by the early 1920s” and “bison raised in captivity were reintroduced there in the 1950s.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and shows the contrast between them.

A.why_wrong: When a coordinating conjunction joins two main clauses of this length, a comma is conventionally placed before it.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses; the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Białowieża Forest, European bison reintroduced from captive herds in the 1950s). Easy: comma + but key with the standard splice / fused / conjunction-without-comma trio.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: Pamukkale, a hillside in southwestern Turkey, is covered in brilliant white terraces of a sedimentary stone called travertine. Because the water from the area’s hot springs is rich in dissolved calcium ______ leaves behind a layer of white mineral deposits as it trickles down the slope.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence opens with the dependent clause “Because the water from the area’s hot springs is rich in dissolved calcium carbonate,” which is followed by the main clause “it leaves behind a layer of white mineral deposits as it trickles down the slope.” A comma correctly separates an introductory dependent clause from the main clause.

B.why_wrong: “And” would join the dependent “because” clause to “it leaves behind ...” as if they were parallel, leaving the sentence with no main clause.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “Because the water ... is rich in dissolved calcium carbonate” is a dependent clause.

D.why_wrong: The period makes “Because the water from the area’s hot springs is rich in dissolved calcium carbonate” a separate sentence, but a dependent clause can’t stand alone.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Pamukkale travertine terraces, Turkey). Easy: Because-clause intro (1.6 shape), with the added-and decoy of 1.6 and the strong-mark fragments of 1.8.

items.subtype: Direct question after a colon: inverted order and question mark
items.passage: During some economic downturns, sales of lipstick and other small luxuries have held steady or even increased while spending on big purchases declined. This pattern, sometimes called the lipstick effect, raises a question: Why ______ One explanation is that small treats feel indulgent without costing much.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: do shoppers keep buying small luxuries when money is tight.
shoppers keep buying small luxuries when money is tight?
do shoppers keep buying small luxuries when money is tight?
shoppers keep buying small luxuries when money is tight.
items.explanation: The colon introduces a direct question that begins with “Why.” A direct question puts the helping verb before the subject (“do shoppers keep buying”) and ends with a question mark.

A.recipe: question errors (direct question ending in a period)
A.why_wrong: The word order is that of a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark, not a period.

B.recipe: question errors (statement order with a question mark)
B.why_wrong: A direct question introduced by “Why” needs the helping verb “do” before the subject; “shoppers keep buying” is statement order.

D.recipe: question errors (direct question left as a statement)
D.why_wrong: This is statement order with a period, but the text introduces a direct question (“raises a question: Why”), which needs question order and a question mark.

items.notes: Subject: social science and economics (the lipstick effect in recessions). Easy: direct question after a colon (1.18 shape), the full 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark; a following sentence starts with a capital so the end mark matters.

items.subtype: Comma before a nonrestrictive which clause
items.passage: California grunion have an unusual reproductive strategy: they leave the water to spawn. On spring and summer nights following the highest tides, females wriggle tail-first into wet sand to deposit their ______ hatch approximately ten days later, when the next high tides wash them out to sea.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “females wriggle tail-first into wet sand to deposit their eggs” is followed by a relative clause, “which hatch approximately ten days later ...,” that adds information about the eggs. A comma correctly sets off this supplementary clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses, but “which hatch approximately ten days later ...” is a relative clause, not a main clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Which hatch approximately ten days later ...” a separate sentence, but a relative clause can’t stand alone.

D.why_wrong: A colon introduces an explanation or list, not a relative clause that describes “eggs.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (California grunion beach spawning). Easy: trailing which clause (1.32 shape).

items.subtype: Semicolon between independent clauses
items.passage: Fourteenth-century poet Hafez remains one of Iran’s most widely read writers. Many families keep a copy of his collected poems, the Divan, at ______ they consult it on special occasions, opening the book at random and interpreting the poem they find as personal guidance.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence joins two main clauses, “Many families keep a copy of his collected poems, the Divan, at home” and “they consult it on special occasions, opening the book at random and interpreting the poem they find as personal guidance.” A semicolon is used to join two main clauses without a conjunction.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two main clauses; the result is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: When “and” joins two main clauses of this length, a comma is conventionally placed before it; without one, the sentence is not punctuated correctly.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses are fused into a run-on sentence.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Hafez's Divan opened at random for guidance, fal-e Hafez). Easy: semicolon key, menu of 1.4 (comma, no mark, and without comma); second clause opens with a pronoun subject. No period option (it would be a twin).
